stars.label: Vibration and pitch
stars.title: Vibration and pitch
stars.body: Every sound starts with something moving back and forth: a violin string, a clarinet reed, the air inside a flute, your own vocal folds. The number of times it moves back and forth each second is its frequency, measured in hertz (Hz). We hear frequency as pitch. The A that orchestras tune to moves 440 times a second, and the A an octave below moves 220 times. When you pluck a string the sound gets quieter as it fades, but the pitch stays the same, because the string keeps the same rhythm while its movement gets smaller.

sources.t: What is music? Module 1, the oscillator and Lab 1

stars.label: Sound in the air
stars.title: Sound in the air
stars.body: A vibrating string pushes the air next to it, squeezing it and letting it go. These small changes of pressure pass from one bit of air to the next and travel outwards at about 343 metres per second. That travelling pattern is sound. The air itself does not travel to your ear, only the pattern does. The size of the pressure changes decides how loud the sound is, measured in decibels. The distance from one squeeze to the next is the wavelength: about 78 cm for the A at 440 Hz, and more than 12 metres for the lowest note of a piano.

sources.t: What is music? Module 1, sound in air and decibels

stars.label: Strings and pipes
stars.title: Strings and pipes
stars.body: A string is fixed at both ends, so the ends cannot move. The only vibrations that last are the ones that fit exactly between the two ends: one half-wave, two half-waves, three, and so on. Each of these shapes has its own frequency, 1, 2, 3… times the lowest one. The air inside a wind instrument follows the same rule with its own boundaries. A flute is open at both ends and holds all the harmonics. A clarinet is closed at one end and holds mostly the odd ones, which is part of why it sounds so different.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Harmonic series (music)
What is music? Module 2, fitting waves on a string

stars.label: The harmonic series
stars.title: The harmonic series
stars.body: When you play one note on a violin, the string vibrates as a whole and, at the same time, in halves, thirds, quarters and smaller parts. So one note is really a stack of frequencies, 1, 2, 3, 4… times the lowest one. These are the harmonics, and together they form the harmonic series. On a low C they give C, C an octave up, G, C again, E, G, a slightly flat B flat, and then they keep climbing, closer and closer together. Octaves, fifths, chords, timbre and the way the ear judges smoothness all come back to this series.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Harmonic series (music)
What is music? Module 2, the harmonic series

stars.label: Timbre
stars.title: Timbre
stars.body: Timbre is the colour of a sound. It is why a violin and a flute playing the same A, equally loud, still sound like two different instruments. The main difference is in the harmonics: each instrument has its own balance of strong and weak ones. A bowed string has many strong upper harmonics, which makes it bright. A flute has fewer, so it sounds rounder. The beginning of the sound matters too. If you cut the attack off a recording, a piano and a trumpet become surprisingly hard to tell apart.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Harmonic series (music)
What is music? Module 2, colour as a recipe of harmonics and Lab 2

stars.label: Resonance and formants
stars.title: Resonance and formants
stars.body: Every object and every hollow space has frequencies at which it vibrates most easily. These are its resonances. When a sound contains those frequencies, the object picks them up and makes them stronger. Your mouth and throat form a space like this, and their resonances are called formants. When you change from ee to ah, your vocal folds keep the same pitch, but your tongue and lips move the formants, and that is what changes the vowel. The wooden body of a violin and the gourds under the keys of a balafon do the same job for their instruments.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Formant
What is music? Module 9, the source and the filter

stars.label: Rooms and reverberation
stars.title: Rooms and reverberation
stars.body: A room is part of every performance. The sound reaches you first directly, and then many more times as it bounces off the walls, the floor and the ceiling. The time a sound takes to fade away after the player stops is called the reverberation time. Around 1900 the physicist Wallace Sabine worked out that it grows with the volume of the room and gets shorter the more the surfaces absorb, with curtains, seats or people. Good concert halls for orchestral music have about two seconds. A small carpeted room has much less, and a stone church can have several seconds, which changes how fast you can play.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Reverberation
What is music? Module 9, the room as the last instrument

stars.label: Ratios
stars.title: Ratios
stars.body: If you halve a string, it sounds exactly an octave higher. Its frequency has doubled, so the two notes are in the ratio 2 to 1. This is the oldest idea in music theory: intervals are ratios of frequencies. The octave is 2:1, the fifth 3:2, the fourth 4:3 and the major third 5:4. To put one interval on top of another, you multiply their ratios. A fifth plus a fourth is 3/2 × 4/3 = 2, exactly an octave, and you can check this on any instrument.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Harmonic series (music)
What is music? Module 0, T1 ratios

stars.label: Logarithms and cents
stars.title: Logarithms and cents
stars.body: Since intervals combine by multiplying, it is hard to compare their sizes directly. Logarithms help, because they turn multiplication into addition. Musicians use a logarithmic unit called the cent. An octave is 1200 cents and each semitone of the piano is exactly 100. A pure fifth, ratio 3:2, is about 702 cents, and the piano's fifth is 700, so they differ by two cents, a fiftieth of a semitone. Most listeners only start to notice differences of around five to ten cents.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Cent (music)
What is music? Module 0, T2 logarithms and the converter

stars.label: Fourier's idea
stars.title: Fourier's idea
stars.body: In the early 1800s Joseph Fourier showed that any wave that repeats, however complicated its shape, can be built by adding simple sine waves. The frequencies of these sine waves are whole-number multiples of how often the wave repeats. For sound, this means that the shape of the wave over time and the list of its harmonics describe the same thing in two ways. A spectrum, the picture that shows how strong each harmonic is, is the second way of looking at it.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Fourier series
What is music? Module 2, Fourier's theorem

stars.label: Primes and commas
stars.title: Primes and commas
stars.body: Every whole number can be written as a product of prime numbers in only one way: 12 is 2 × 2 × 3 and nothing else. This simple fact has a musical consequence. Octaves are built from the number 2 and fifths from the number 3. However many fifths you stack, you get powers of 3, and these can never equal a power of 2. So a chain of pure fifths never lands exactly on an octave, and every tuning has a small leftover, which musicians call a comma.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Pythagorean comma
What is music? Module 4, why pure fifths can never close the circle

stars.label: Continued fractions
stars.title: Continued fractions
stars.body: A continued fraction is a method to find the simplest fractions that come closest to a given number. In music, the number to approximate is the size of the fifth measured in octaves, about 0.585. The method gives the fractions 3/5, 7/12, 24/41 and 31/53, each closer than the one before. The bottom number of each fraction is a number of equal notes per octave that contains a good fifth. Twelve is on the list, and it is the first one where the fifth is so close to pure that most people cannot hear the difference.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Equal temperament
What is music? Module 5, running the continued fraction by hand

stars.label: Clock arithmetic
stars.title: Clock arithmetic
stars.body: Number the twelve notes of the octave like the hours of a clock, with C at twelve o'clock. After B comes C again, as after eleven comes twelve. Arithmetic on this circle wraps around, and it describes music well. A fifth is seven steps, and if you keep adding seven you visit all twelve notes before coming back to C. The same circle works for rhythm: place the twelve pulses of a cycle around it and mark where the drum or the bell plays.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Euclidean rhythm
What is music? Module 6, counting the gaps on the piano

stars.label: The cochlea
stars.title: The cochlea
stars.body: The cochlea is a small coiled tube in the inner ear, about the size of a pea. Inside it runs a membrane that is narrow and stiff at one end and wider and looser at the other. High frequencies make the stiff end vibrate and low frequencies the loose end, so each place along the membrane responds to its own range of pitches. In this way the ear separates a sound into its frequencies before the signal reaches the brain, a little like a prism separates light into colours.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Cochlea
What is music? Module 1, the ear as a spectrum analyser

stars.label: Beats
stars.title: Beats
stars.body: When two notes are very close in pitch, for example two violin strings that are almost in tune, their vibrations go in and out of step. When they are in step they add up and the sound gets louder, and when they are out of step they cancel and it gets softer. You hear one note pulsing: wah, wah, wah. The number of pulses per second is the difference between the two frequencies, so the closer the notes, the slower the pulsing. Musicians use this to tune: they adjust until the beats slow down and disappear.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Beat (acoustics)
What is music? Module 3, the wobble between two close notes and Lab 3a

stars.label: Roughness and consonance
stars.title: Roughness and consonance
stars.body: When two notes are a little further apart, the beats become too fast to count, and the sound turns grainy or buzzy. This is roughness. In 1863 Hermann Helmholtz proposed that it explains why some intervals sound smooth and others tense. With simple ratios like the octave and the fifth, many harmonics of the two notes coincide exactly. With an interval like the semitone, many harmonics land close to each other and rub. Whether people enjoy roughness is another question. Some traditions look for it, and listeners who grew up far from Western music do not always prefer the smooth intervals. verify

sources.t: Wikipedia: Consonance and dissonance
Plomp and Levelt (1965), Tonal consonance and critical bandwidth, JASA 38, 548 to 560
McDermott et al. (2016), Indifference to dissonance in native Amazonians, Nature 535, 547 to 550
What is music? Module 3, why some intervals sound smooth and Lab 3b

stars.label: The missing fundamental
stars.title: The missing fundamental
stars.body: Play a note through a filter that removes its lowest harmonic and keeps harmonics 2 to 6. You might expect the pitch to jump up, but it does not: you still hear the original low note. The brain recognises the pattern of the harmonics, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 times the same frequency, and hears that frequency as the pitch, even though nothing is sounding there. This is why a small phone speaker, which cannot produce low frequencies, still lets you follow a bass line.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Missing fundamental
What is music? Module 1, Lab 1 missing-fundamental buttons

stars.label: The octave
stars.title: The octave
stars.body: Two notes an octave apart, with frequencies in the ratio 2:1, sound so similar that most musical traditions treat them as the same note. When men and women sing a song together, they usually sing an octave apart without noticing. The physics helps explain why: all the harmonics of the upper note are already harmonics of the lower one, so the two blend almost completely. This is why the octave is the frame in which most scales are built.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Harmonic series (music)
What is music? Module 6, the octave, the same note again

stars.label: The fifth
stars.title: The fifth
stars.body: The fifth, ratio 3:2, is the most consonant interval after the octave. Harmonic 3 of the lower note has the same frequency as harmonic 2 of the upper one, and when the fifth is pure that shared harmonic sounds steady, without beats. This makes the fifth easy to tune by ear, and violinists tune their four strings this way. Theorists in China, Greece, India and the Arab world all used chains of fifths to build their notes.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Harmonic series (music)
Wikipedia: Shí-èr-lǜ (Chinese twelve pitches)
What is music? Module 6, the fifth, the easiest interval to tune and Lab 6

stars.label: The Pythagorean comma
stars.title: The Pythagorean comma
stars.body: Start on a note and go up by twelve pure fifths. You pass through all twelve notes of the piano and arrive near the starting note, seven octaves higher. But not exactly: you overshoot by about 23.5 cents, almost a quarter of a semitone. This small difference is the Pythagorean comma. Because of it, an instrument with fixed notes, like a piano or an organ, cannot have all its fifths and all its octaves perfectly pure at the same time.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Pythagorean comma
What is music? Module 4, primes and commas

stars.label: Temperament
stars.title: Temperament
stars.body: A temperament is a decision about where to put the comma. Pythagorean tuning keeps eleven fifths pure and puts the whole comma in the last one, which sounds so out of tune that it is called the wolf. Meantone tunings narrow the fifths further so that the major thirds are pure, which suited Renaissance music beautifully. The well temperaments of Bach's time spread the comma unevenly, so each key had its own colour. Equal temperament, the modern piano tuning, makes every fifth two cents narrow, so all keys sound alike.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Equal temperament
What is music? Module 5, tuning and temperament and Lab 5a

stars.label: Twelve notes
stars.title: Twelve notes
stars.body: Why does the piano have twelve notes in each octave? If you build notes by going up in fifths, after twelve steps you come back very close to where you started, so twelve notes make an almost closed circle. Twelve is also small enough to fit under the hands. Fewer notes would give poor fifths, and many more would be hard to play and to learn. On the keyboard, the seven white keys come from the first seven fifths, and the five black keys fill the gaps with the next five.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Equal temperament
What is music? Module 6, why the octave has twelve notes

stars.label: Pentatonic and diatonic
stars.title: Pentatonic and diatonic
stars.body: If you stop the chain of fifths after five notes, you get the pentatonic scale, the five notes of the black keys. It appears in songs from China, Scotland, West Africa and the Andes. If you stop after seven notes, you get the diatonic scale, the white keys. Both scales have something in common: their steps come in only two sizes, so the notes are spread fairly evenly around the octave. This may be one reason why they are easy to sing and remember, and why they appear in so many places.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Mode (music)
What is music? Module 6, why five and seven appear everywhere

stars.label: Modes, major and minor
stars.title: Modes, major and minor
stars.body: The seven white keys can give seven different modes, depending on which note feels like home. Starting and ending on C gives the major mode (Ionian), on D the Dorian mode, on A the minor mode (Aeolian), and so on. The notes are the same, but the character changes. Medieval and Renaissance music used all of them. From the 1600s Western music relied mainly on major and minor, which give a strong ending through the leading tone, the note just below home. Folk music, jazz and film music kept using the others.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Mode (music)
What is music? Module 6, same notes, a different home

stars.label: Chords and voice leading
stars.title: Chords and voice leading
stars.body: A major chord is already present inside a single note: harmonics 4, 5 and 6 of a low C are C, E and G. When one chord follows another, musicians usually prefer that each voice moves as little as possible to its next note. This is called voice leading. In 1739 Leonhard Euler drew a map of notes, later called the Tonnetz, where chords that share two notes sit next to each other. On this map, smooth progressions are short walks.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Harmonic series (music)
What is music? Module 7, harmony and voice leading and Lab 7b

stars.label: Rhythm and polyrhythm
stars.title: Rhythm and polyrhythm
stars.body: Rhythm and pitch are closer than they seem. A drum played four times a second is a rhythm. Speed it up to a hundred times a second and you hear a low note. In the same way, three beats against two, a polyrhythm, becomes a fifth when it is sped up, because the fifth is the ratio 3:2. Another link with mathematics is in how strokes are spread round a cycle: placing them as evenly as possible gives many of the bell patterns of West Africa and Cuba.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Euclidean rhythm
What is music? Module 8, rhythm, time and cycles and Lab 8a

stars.label: Notation
stars.title: Notation
stars.body: Every way of writing music decides what to keep and what to leave to the performer. The Western staff is a kind of graph, with pitch going up and time going to the right. Note values are fractions: half notes, quarter notes, eighth notes. Other systems write scale numbers, as in Chinese jianpu, syllables, as in Indian sargam, or finger positions, as in lute and guitar tablature. Many traditions do not write music at all and pass it on by ear, from teacher to student.

sources.t: What is music? Module 11, writing sound down

stars.label: Gamelan and ombak
stars.title: Gamelan and ombak
stars.body: Gamelan orchestras from Java and Bali are made mostly of bronze metallophones and gongs. Bronze bars do not have neatly spaced harmonics like strings, so the intervals that sound good on them are different. Gamelans use two scale systems, sléndro with five notes and pélog with seven, and each set of instruments is tuned to itself, so no two gamelans sound exactly alike. In Bali, instruments are made in pairs tuned slightly apart, so that together they beat and shimmer. This effect is called ombak, which means wave.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Gamelan
What is music? Module 3, nature or culture

stars.label: Rāga and śruti
stars.title: Rāga and śruti
stars.body: A rāga is much more than a scale. It also says which notes are used going up and which going down, which notes are important, which phrases are typical and how each note is ornamented. Some rāgas are linked to a time of day or a season. Indian musicians tune each note by listening against the drone of the tanpura, and the old theory describes 22 small steps in the octave, called śruti. Time is organised in rhythmic cycles called tāla.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Raga
What is music? Module 6, other worlds of scale

stars.label: Maqām and makam
stars.title: Maqām and makam
stars.body: Arab maqām and Turkish makam are systems of melodic modes, each with its own notes, typical phrases and path through the scale. Many of them use intervals that fall between the keys of the piano, such as a neutral third, halfway between minor and major. Arab theory often writes them on a grid of 24 quarter tones per octave, and Turkish theory on a grid of 53 small steps. In practice, the exact pitch of these notes changes from one maqām to another and from region to region, and it is learned by ear from a teacher.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Arabic maqam
What is music? Module 4, neutral intervals

stars.label: Overtone and undertone singing
stars.title: Overtone and undertone singing
stars.body: In overtone singing, a singer holds one low note and shapes the mouth and tongue so that one harmonic becomes much louder than the others. It sounds like a second voice whistling a melody above the drone. The tradition is strong in Tuva and Mongolia, and among Xhosa women in South Africa. Some Tibetan monks chant with a very deep undertone: a second pair of folds in the throat vibrates together with the vocal folds and adds a note an octave below.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Overtone singing
What is music? Module 9, singing the harmonics themselves

stars.label: West African timelines
stars.title: West African timelines
stars.body: In Ewe music from Ghana and Togo, and in many other West African traditions, a bell plays a repeating pattern called a timeline. A common one has seven strokes spread over twelve pulses. Everyone in the ensemble listens to it to stay together, while the drums play patterns of three and two against each other around it. Through the Atlantic slave trade these patterns travelled to the Americas, and you can hear them in Cuban and Brazilian music today.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Euclidean rhythm
What is music? Module 8, spreading beats as evenly as possible

stars.label: Andean siku
stars.title: Andean siku
stars.body: The siku is the Andean panpipe. It is divided into two rows of pipes, called ira and arka, and each row is played by a different person. Neither row has all the notes, so the two players alternate to make one melody between them. Sikuri ensembles play the same melody on pipes of different sizes at the same time, often an octave apart, which gives a thick, breathy sound. Each pipe is closed at the bottom, so, like a clarinet, it sounds mostly the odd harmonics.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Siku (instrument)
What is music? Module 7, hocket and parallel voices

stars.label: Harmony of the spheres
stars.title: Harmony of the spheres
stars.body: The idea that the sky is a kind of music goes back to the Pythagoreans in ancient Greece. In 1619 Johannes Kepler published Harmonices Mundi, where he showed that for each planet, the ratio between its fastest and slowest speed around the Sun is close to a musical interval: about a major third for Saturn and a fifth for Mars. Today astronomers find simple ratios in real orbits, called orbital resonances, and they study stars by measuring how they vibrate, a little like listening to a bell.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Musica universalis
What is music? Module 10, harmony of the cosmos and Lab 10

stars.label: Music
stars.title: What is music?
stars.body: A way into music through many doors: the physics of sound, the mathematics of ratios, the ear, tuning and harmony, and the traditions and arts of the world. Each line between two ideas reads in both directions, and the two readings differ.

sources.t: What is music? A course through many lenses

links: The vibration is where the sound begins. The string moves, the air next to it is squeezed and released, and that pattern travels to your ear. It keeps the same frequency all the way, which is why the pitch you hear is the pitch the string is playing.

A vibration only becomes sound when it moves the air. A string vibrating in empty space would make no sound. Even in air, a thin string moves very little air by itself, which is why a violin has a wooden body: it picks up the vibration and pushes much more air.

A string is one particular vibrating object, with a strong limit: its two ends cannot move. That limit decides which vibrations are possible, and so which frequencies the string can play. Change its length, its tension or its thickness and those frequencies change too.

On a string, a vibration is never one simple movement. When you pluck or bow it, the string moves as a whole and also in halves, thirds and quarters at the same time. What looks like one vibration is several, all happening together.

The harmonic series is the list of vibrations that fit on a string between its two fixed ends: one half-wave, two, three and so on. Their frequencies are 1, 2, 3 times the lowest one. So the series follows directly from the shape of the string.

A string is a very good instrument for hearing the harmonic series one note at a time. If you touch a violin string lightly at its middle and bow, you hear harmonic 2, an octave up. Touch it at a third of its length and you hear harmonic 3. String players call these natural harmonics and use them all the time.

Timbre depends on how much of each harmonic a sound contains. Two notes with the same pitch have the same harmonics, with different strengths. If you change the balance, for example by bowing closer to the bridge, which makes the upper harmonics stronger, the same note changes colour.

Normally we do not hear the harmonics of a note one by one. We hear them blended together as the voice of an instrument. With practice, and in a quiet room, you can start to pick some of them out, especially the octave and the fifth above the note.

Fourier's theorem says that what happens on a string happens in any steady sound. Every note that repeats can be split into harmonics at whole-number multiples of its frequency. So the harmonic series appears in voices, wind instruments and synthesisers as well as in strings.

From Fourier's point of view, the harmonic series follows from mathematics. A wave that repeats f times per second can only contain the frequencies f, 2f, 3f and so on, because any other frequency would break the repetition.

Fourier's idea gives a way to measure the colour of a sound. A spectrum shows how strong each harmonic is. If you compare the spectra of a violin and a flute playing the same note, you can see on the graph what you hear as the difference between them.

The same harmonics with different strengths add up to a wave with a different shape. The ear hears that difference as colour, although it follows the strengths of the harmonics more closely than the exact shape of the wave.

Resonances shape the timbre of most instruments. The body of a violin or the mouth of a singer makes some harmonics louder and others softer. That is why the same string, put on two different violins, can sound quite different.

Think of a sound as a source and a filter. Your vocal folds produce a buzz full of harmonics, the same for every vowel. The shape of your mouth and throat, the filter, decides which harmonics come out loudest. When you move your tongue the filter changes, and you hear a different vowel.

A room behaves like a very large resonator. It reflects some frequencies more than others and keeps the sound going after the player stops. In a small room some bass notes can boom, because they match the room's own resonances.

Each resonance of a room comes from sound bouncing back and forth between its walls and reinforcing itself. In a large hall there are so many of these resonances that they merge into a smooth reverberation, and Sabine's formula tells how long it lasts.

Overtone singing uses a resonance so precisely that it picks out one single harmonic. The singer keeps the same low note and moves the tongue to place a resonance of the mouth on harmonic 8, then 9, then 10. Each harmonic becomes a note of the melody.

Overtone singers show that a formant can be played like an instrument. The voice holds one pitch the whole time, and the melody comes entirely from moving the resonances of the mouth, which most of us do without thinking when we change vowels.

In overtone singing, the harmonic series can be heard as a melody. The whistled notes can only be harmonics of the low note being held, so the scale the singer uses is the harmonic series itself, mostly harmonics 6 to 12.

Overtone singing makes the harmonic series audible. Over a low A at 110 Hz, harmonics 6 to 12 are at 660, 770, 880 Hz and higher, a bright melody far above the held note. From harmonic 8 upwards they are close enough together to form a scale.

The cochlea is where the pressure wave in the air becomes a signal in the nerves. Through the eardrum and three tiny bones, the wave reaches the fluid inside the cochlea and makes its membrane move. Each place along the membrane answers to a different frequency.

A sound wave reaches the ear as one complicated movement of the eardrum. The cochlea separates it into its frequencies, each at its own place along the membrane. So the ear does a kind of frequency analysis before the brain does anything else.

Beats happen when two notes are so close that they shake the same place on the membrane of the cochlea. There they add up and cancel each other in turn, and we hear the loudness rise and fall. Notes far enough apart shake different places, and we hear them as two separate notes.

Beats show that the cochlea has a limit to how finely it separates frequencies. Two tones close enough to share one region of the membrane beat; two tones further apart are heard as two notes. The width of these regions is called the critical band.

The missing fundamental shows that hearing goes beyond the cochlea. The membrane receives harmonics 2 to 6 and nothing at the lowest frequency, so no place on it responds to that pitch. Still, the brain reports the low note, because it fits the pattern of what does arrive.

The cochlea splits a sound into its parts, and the brain puts them back together. The missing fundamental is one of the clearest examples of this second step: the pitch we hear is built in the brain from the pattern of the harmonics.
The brain recognises the harmonic series as a pattern. Notes at 220, 330 and 440 Hz are harmonics 2, 3 and 4 of 110 Hz, so the brain hears 110 Hz, even when nothing at 110 Hz is sounding.

Harmonics do more than colour a sound. They also carry its pitch, so strongly that the lowest harmonic can be removed and we still hear the same note. A bass line on a small phone speaker is an everyday example.

Roughness is what beats become when they are too fast to count. From around fifteen to twenty beats per second, the pulsing turns into a buzz or a grain in the sound. Two notes a semitone apart around middle C sound like this.

Slow beats are the gentle end of roughness, and musicians use them in different ways. A piano tuner listens for them in order to remove them. An accordion maker tunes pairs of reeds slightly apart to create them, and many organs have a stop, the voix céleste, made for this effect.

Whether two notes sound rough together depends on their harmonics. If many harmonics of one note land close to harmonics of the other without matching, they beat fast and the interval sounds rough. A pure sine wave has no harmonics, so the same intervals sound much less rough with sine waves.

The harmonic series gives a simple reason why some intervals sound smooth. When two notes are in a simple ratio, many of their harmonics have exactly the same frequency, so they do not beat. In an octave, every harmonic of the upper note matches one of the lower note.

The fifth sounds smooth because harmonic 3 of the lower note and harmonic 2 of the upper note have the same frequency, and so do harmonics 6 and 4, and 9 and 6. The harmonics that do not match stay far enough apart not to rub.

Musicians use roughness when they tune fifths. If the fifth is slightly out of tune, the shared harmonic beats slowly. As the player turns the peg, the beats slow down and stop when the fifth is pure. This is how violinists tune their strings.

In Balinese gamelan, roughness is chosen on purpose. Instruments come in pairs, one tuned slightly higher than the other, so that together they beat at a steady rate. This shimmer, ombak, is part of the sound the musicians want, and each gamelan has its own speed of ombak.

Gamelan shows that liking or avoiding roughness depends on culture as well as on physics. The beating that a piano tuner works to remove is what a Balinese tuner aims for. Studies with listeners from very different musical backgrounds also suggest that the preference for smooth intervals is partly learned.
As a ratio, the octave is the simplest interval after the unison: 2 to 1. Halve the length of a string and its frequency doubles.

Because octaves sound like the same note, they give ratios a frame. You can multiply or divide any ratio by 2 without changing the name of the note. That is how a ratio like 9/4 becomes 9/8, the whole tone, inside one octave.
The fifth is the ratio 3 to 2, the next simplest after the octave. On a string, two thirds of its length sounds a fifth higher than the whole string.

With the fifth, ratios become a way to build notes. Start on a note and multiply by 3/2 again and again, bringing each new note back into the octave by dividing by 2. The notes of a scale appear one after another. Pythagorean and early Chinese tunings were built this way.

Ratios combine by multiplying, which makes it hard to compare intervals or add them in your head. Logarithms turn ratios into sizes you can add, measured in cents. A fifth of 702 cents and a fourth of 498 cents add up to 1200, one octave.

With logarithms, every ratio becomes a length on a ruler, and the ruler is the same in every octave. 3/2 is 702 cents, 4/3 is 498, 5/4 is 386. You can compare them directly with the 100-cent steps of the piano.

The cochlea works roughly like a logarithmic ruler. Above a few hundred hertz, each octave takes up about the same length of the membrane, wherever it is. This is one reason we hear intervals as ratios: an octave sounds like the same distance, low or high.

The logarithm is built into the ear. When you go up an octave, the place of strongest vibration moves along the cochlea by about the same distance, whether you start low or high. The cents that musicians use follow the ear in this way.
The fifth divides the octave into two unequal parts. A fifth up and then a fourth up make exactly one octave, 3/2 × 4/3 = 2. That is why the fourth is called the inversion of the fifth.
If you keep stacking fifths, you keep almost reaching an octave. Twelve fifths nearly make seven octaves, but they overshoot by a small amount, so the chain never quite closes.

The comma is the cost of stacking pure fifths. After twelve of them, the note you reach is about a quarter of a semitone higher than seven octaves above the start. On a violin you can adjust as you play, but on a keyboard this small difference has to go somewhere.

Because of the comma, every fifth on a keyboard is a compromise. If all the fifths are pure, one of them becomes very out of tune. If each one is narrowed a little, none of them is perfectly pure. On the modern piano each fifth is two cents narrow.

Prime numbers show that the comma cannot be avoided. Stacking fifths gives powers of 3 and stacking octaves gives powers of 2. Since every whole number has only one prime factorisation, no power of 3 can ever equal a power of 2, so the two chains never meet exactly.
The comma is a place where you can hear a property of numbers. The 3 in the ratio of the fifth never cancels out, and after twelve fifths you hear the result as a note that is slightly too high.

Every temperament is a way of dealing with the comma. Each one spreads the 23.5 cents differently among the fifths, and tuners in different centuries made different choices depending on the music they played.

For a tuner, the comma is something to share out. Pythagorean tuning puts all of it in one fifth, the wolf. Equal temperament takes about two cents from each of the twelve fifths. Historical tunings found many ways in between.

Continued fractions show that twelve is a very good choice. The fifth is 0.585 of an octave, and 7/12 is the closest fraction with a small denominator. Seven steps out of twelve give a fifth only two cents away from pure.

Continued fractions help explain the number twelve. The method lists 5, 12, 41 and 53 as the numbers of equal steps that give the best fifths. Five is too rough, and 41 or 53 are a lot of notes to play, so twelve is the practical choice. Turkish theory uses the 53.
To use continued fractions on a musical interval, you first need its size in octaves, which is a logarithm. For the fifth it is log₂(3/2) = 0.58496…, and this is the number the method approximates.
Logarithms turn the search for a good tuning into a simple question: how many equal steps in an octave put one of them very close to 702 cents? Continued fractions answer it.

Deciding to have twelve notes per octave does not yet say how to tune them. Twelve keys can be tuned so that the fifths are pure, or the thirds, or so that all keys are equal. That choice is the work of temperament.

Temperament becomes a practical problem once an instrument has only twelve fixed notes. Singers and violinists can adjust each note as they play. A keyboard cannot, so the comma has to be placed somewhere.
In an octave of twelve equal steps, the fifth is seven steps, 700 cents. That is only two cents narrower than a pure fifth, which most people cannot hear.

The twelve notes come from the fifth. Start on F, go up in fifths and bring each note back into the octave: F, C, G, D, A, E, B, then F sharp, C sharp, G sharp, D sharp and A sharp. After twelve steps you are almost back at F.

The most common scales choose some of the twelve notes. The pentatonic uses five, like the black keys, and the diatonic uses seven, like the white keys. Most melodies stay within five or seven notes at a time.

The twelve notes are the full set that scales choose from. Changing key means choosing a different set of seven from the same twelve, which works so easily because on the modern piano the twelve are evenly spaced.
On the clock of twelve notes, a scale is a set of hours. Start at F and add fifths, seven hours at a time. Five steps give the pentatonic scale, and seven give the major scale.
The clock shows why these scales sound balanced. The major scale is the most even way to place seven notes among twelve hours, and the pentatonic is the most even way to place five.

On the clock, adding seven over and over visits every one of the twelve hours before coming back. This works because 7 and 12 have no common factor. With steps of 6 you would only ever visit two hours.
Twelve notes fit naturally on a clock. After B comes C again, just as after eleven comes twelve. This is why musicians draw the circle of fifths as a clock face.

On a clock of pulses, a rhythm is a set of points where something is played. Spread seven strokes as evenly as possible over twelve pulses and you get one of the most common West African bell patterns.
The clock that organises scales also organises time. The bell pattern of seven strokes in twelve pulses has exactly the same shape as the major scale on the twelve-note clock.
A mode is a scale with a chosen home note. The seven white keys give seven modes, depending on which note feels like the end of the melody.

A scale is a set of notes, and it becomes music once it has a home and a way of moving. The same seven notes can sound bright, as in major, or dark, as in Phrygian, depending on where the melody rests.
Chords help explain why major and minor became the main modes in Western music. Both can end with a strong cadence: a dominant chord whose leading tone pulls up into the home note.

Each mode gives different chords. In major, the chord on the fifth note contains the leading tone, which pulls strongly home. Dorian and Mixolydian have no leading tone, so to get the same strong ending musicians raised a note, and over time this turned these modes towards major and minor.
The harmonic series contains the major chord. Harmonics 4, 5 and 6 of a low C are C, E and G, in the ratio 4:5:6.
A chord can be heard as one note spread out. In 1722 Jean-Philippe Rameau argued that harmony grows from this natural chord inside every note, and he built his theory of the root of a chord on it.

In harmony, roughness is a colour that composers place on purpose. A dominant seventh chord is rough and seems to want to move, and the chord it moves to is smoother. Much of Western harmony is built on this movement from tension to rest.

Choirs use roughness to tune their chords. In a major chord, singers lower the third about 14 cents below the piano's third. At that point its harmonics match those of the other notes, the beats disappear and the chord rings.

A rāga uses a scale, and adds much more: rules for going up and coming down, notes to stress or avoid, typical phrases and ornaments. Two rāgas can use exactly the same notes and still be clearly different music.
In Indian music, the scale is the basic material of a rāga. Carnatic theory lists 72 parent scales, the melakarta, and thousands of rāgas are derived from them.

Andean music is a good place to hear the pentatonic scale in everyday use. Many traditional melodies of the Altiplano are pentatonic, and more recent songs often move between pentatonic, major and minor.
On the siku, a scale is shared by two players. Each row of the panpipe holds every other note, so neither player can play the whole scale alone, and the melody only exists when both play.

Maqām keeps the notes that fall between the piano keys. A grid of 24 or 53 steps per octave is a way of writing these notes down, but musicians place them by ear, and their exact height depends on the maqām and the region.
From the point of view of maqām, equal temperament is one possible choice among many. With twelve equal notes, the neutral intervals that give maqām Rast or Bayātī their character cannot be played.

Gamelan tuning goes against the idea of one standard. Each set of instruments is tuned to itself, and musicians value the differences between gamelans. A single universal tuning would remove what makes each one recognisable.

Gamelan shows that the best tuning depends on the instrument. Bronze bars and gongs have harmonics that are not evenly spaced, so the intervals that sound smooth on them are different from those of strings or voices.

In Indian music, rhythm is organised in tāla, cycles of beats counted with claps and waves of the hand. A common ending, the tihāī, repeats a phrase three times, timed so that the last note lands exactly on the first beat of the cycle, called sam.
Indian rhythm plays across the cycle. Groups of 3, 5 or 7 are placed against the tāla, which builds tension, and the tension is released when the music comes back to sam, the first beat.
West African music layers several beats at the same time. Dancers may follow one layer and musicians another, and the music lives in how the layers fit together.
In West African music, rhythm is a conversation between parts around a fixed bell pattern. Three against two is the normal ground of the music, present almost all the time.
A polyrhythm is a ratio in time. Three beats against two is 3:2. If you speed it up beyond about twenty repetitions per second, the beats become pitches and you hear a perfect fifth.
The same ratio can be heard as a rhythm or as an interval. 3:2 played slowly is a polyrhythm, and played fast it is a fifth. Lab 8a in the course lets you hear the change happen.
Western notation writes time as fractions: halves, quarters and eighths, with dots and triplets for other lengths. The notes in each bar have to add up to the time signature.
Rhythm is the hardest thing to write down completely. The small delays and pushes that make music swing or groove are not in the score, and players learn them by listening.
The staff is a logarithmic graph. Each line or space up is one step of the scale, and an octave takes the same height wherever it is on the staff, as it does along the cochlea.
Notation uses logarithms without saying so. A score places equal intervals at equal heights, which matches the way the ear hears them.
Kepler looked for musical ratios in the sky. He found that the ratio between Saturn's fastest and slowest speed, seen from the Sun, is close to 5:4, a major third, and for Mars close to 3:2, a fifth.

Simple ratios do appear in real orbits. Planets and moons often settle into periods in ratios like 2:1 or 3:2, called orbital resonances. Neptune goes round the Sun three times while Pluto goes round twice.
Resonance reaches the stars. The Sun vibrates in millions of modes at once, and by measuring these vibrations astronomers can see inside it. This field is called helioseismology.

A star vibrates like a huge bell. Measuring its frequencies tells astronomers about its density, its age and its inner layers. The tones are far too low for us to hear, but they can be sped up into sound.

A siku ensemble makes a full sound without chord progressions. Many players sound the same melody together on pipes of different sizes, an octave or more apart, and the richness comes from these layers.
In a siku ensemble, harmony comes from many sizes of pipe playing the same melody together, and from two players sharing one line. It is another way to make many voices sound as one.
To describe maqām precisely you need cents. A neutral third is about 350 cents, halfway between the piano's minor third at 300 and major third at 400, so the piano cannot play it.
With cents, maqām intervals can be compared exactly with other tunings. The Turkish comma is about 22.6 cents, the Arab quarter tone 50 and the Pythagorean comma 23.5.
In gamelan, the timbre of the instruments shapes the tuning. Bronze bars and gongs have harmonics that are not neatly spaced, so the intervals that sound smooth on them move away from simple ratios.
Much of the gamelan's sound comes from the bronze. Its uneven harmonics give the instruments their ringing colour, and they are part of why gamelan scales differ from those of strings and voices.
On a string, a ratio is a length you can measure. Two thirds of the string sounds a fifth higher, three quarters a fourth higher and half an octave higher.
The string was the first instrument of music theory. With a monochord, one string stretched over a ruler, Greek and Chinese theorists measured intervals as lengths.
One idea among many. The map is where it meets the others.
Where the map begins: a way of listening.
